<reason>Side A built a much cleaner, more logically consistent case and systematically dismantled Side B's core objections. Side A effectively showed how pre-lease disclosure solves a severe information asymmetry and creates financial incentives for landlords to fix chronic issues like broken locks or rogue party units. Side B committed a major economic contradiction by arguing that disclosure both depresses value via a "problem building discount" and causes landlords to raise rents to offset it. When pressed by Side A, Side B had to walk that claim back, and Side A cleanly refuted Side B's subsequent pivot about portfolio-wide rent hikes. Side A also neutralised Side B's concerns about fabricated complaints by proposing multi-household corroboration and carrier/police logs, while exposing the false choice between code enforcement and upfront transparency.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's takedown (across [A3.2], [A4.5]-[A4.6], and [A5.3]) of Side B's claim in [B2.3] that landlords would "raise rents to offset the 'problem building' discount," forcing Side B to retract the claim in [B4.2] and concede that disclosure forces a "lemons" discount—which Side A then used to prove that fixing defects becomes the landlord's only profitable move.</best_rebuttal>
